title: Disease and Development: Evidence from Hookworm Eradication in the American South
research_question: What are the long-term economic and human-capital consequences of eliminating a chronic childhood parasitic disease burden? Specifically, does reducing childhood hookworm infection raise school enrollment, attendance, literacy, and adult earnings, and how much of regional underdevelopment can be attributed to such disease burdens?
data_description: The study combines aggregate area-level disease data with individual-level census microdata. Hookworm infection rates for over 600 Southern U.S. counties (1910–1914) come from Rockefeller Sanitary Commission surveys of school-aged children based on stool examinations; state-level infection rates from Kofoid and Tucker (1921) army-recruit data are also used. Individual outcomes are drawn from IPUMS decennial census samples (1880, 1900–1990, plus NAPP 1880), restricted to native-born whites and blacks. Children aged 8–16 are examined for school enrollment, full-time attendance, and literacy; adults aged 25–55 for literacy, labor-force participation, occupational income score, and urban residence; cohorts aged 25–60 in 1940 for wage and salary earnings (1939) and years of schooling. Geographic units are State Economic Areas (county groupings) and state of birth. Additional aggregate controls include school resources, sanitation, mortality, agricultural variables, and parental background.
institutional_context: Around 1910, hookworm disease—a parasitic infection causing anemia, lethargy, and stunted growth, particularly in children—was discovered to be widespread in the American South, with roughly 40 percent of school-aged children infected. Following a $1 million donation from John D. Rockefeller, the Rockefeller Sanitary Commission (RSC) was established in 1910 and conducted a five-year campaign (1910–1915) across more than 600 Southern counties. The campaign surveyed infection rates, sent traveling dispensaries to provide free deworming medication (thymol) to over 400,000 individuals, and educated physicians, teachers, and the public about hygiene and sanitary latrines. State and local health authorities, along with the Rockefeller Foundation's International Health Board, sustained follow-up efforts. Infection rates fell by more than half within roughly a decade. Hookworm prevalence varied geographically due to climate and soil conditions, with sandy, warm coastal-plain areas more affected than piedmont or mountain regions.
